name: Niacinamide
summary: The barrier-support ingredient that makes the rest of a regimen tolerable — genuinely useful, but rarely enough to clear acne on its own.
good: Offsetting dryness/irritation from a retinoid or benzoyl peroxide regimen.
bad: Treating it as a substitute for an actual active ingredient — on its own it rarely clears meaningful acne.
clinicalPearls: Niacinamide’s real job is damage control for the barrier while the retinoid or BPO does the actual clearing work — useful, but a supporting role, not the lead.
mechanism: Mildly sebum-regulating and anti-inflammatory, and directly supports barrier lipid (ceramide) synthesis — a supportive rather than primary comedolytic or antibacterial action.
originalFields: Mildly sebum-regulating and anti-inflammatory, and directly supports barrier lipid (ceramide) synthesis — a supportive rather than primary comedolytic or antibacterial action.
Adjunct for redness/irritation reduction and barrier support alongside more active agents like retinoids or benzoyl peroxide.
Slow and subtle — a maintenance ingredient more than a primary treatment.
Very low — one of the best-tolerated actives available.
Modest evidence for reducing PIH by interfering with melanosome transfer to keratinocytes — weaker than azelaic acid or hydroquinone, but essentially risk-free to add.
Genuinely barrier-supportive — increases ceramide synthesis, which is why it’s frequently paired with more irritating actives.
Primarily leave-on, via serums or moisturizers.
Either — commonly layered under a retinoid or alongside benzoyl peroxide as a buffer.
One of the most combination-friendly ingredients available — no significant incompatibilities.
